clinicalPearls: Characterised by a defect in initiating horizontal voluntary (saccadic) eye movements, with preserved reflexive and vertical movements
Affected children use compensatory horizontal head thrusts, often with a blink, to bring the eyes onto a target
The head characteristically overshoots the target and the eyes then settle, a manoeuvre that lessens with age
May be isolated or a sign of an underlying brain malformation, particularly a Joubert-related disorder with the molar tooth sign
Associated conditions include Joubert syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, the ataxias with oculomotor apraxia and certain metabolic disorders
Early gross motor delay is common, but many children are otherwise developmentally normal
The finding warrants neuroimaging to look for cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and related malformation
reference.pathophysiology: Cogan-type oculomotor apraxia reflects a defect in the supranuclear control of horizontal saccades, the fast eye movements that redirect gaze, while the pathways for reflexive and vertical movements are relatively spared. To compensate, the child throws the head towards a new target, using the intact vestibulo-ocular reflex to drag the eyes across, then re-centres the head once fixation is achieved. In many children the sign is isolated and improves with maturation, but it is frequently a marker of underlying cerebellar and brainstem malformation, especially the molar tooth malformation of Joubert syndrome and related ciliopathies, in which disordered ciliary signalling disturbs mid-hindbrain development. It also occurs in neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders such as ataxia-telangiectasia and the ataxias with oculomotor apraxia, so its recognition should prompt a search for such causes.
additionalDifferentials: Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia types 1 and 2
Delayed visual maturation of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Detailed ophthalmological and orthoptic assessment of saccades and compensatory head thrusts
Brain MRI to look for the molar tooth sign and posterior fossa malformation
Targeted testing for ataxia-telangiectasia or the oculomotor apraxia ataxias where indicated
Ciliopathy gene panel when a Joubert-related disorder is suspected
redFlags: Progressive ataxia or neurological decline suggesting a neurodegenerative cause
Features of ataxia-telangiectasia such as telangiectasia, immune deficiency and cancer predisposition
A molar tooth sign on imaging indicating a Joubert-related disorder
reference.prognosis: When isolated, the compensatory head thrusts tend to lessen with age and the outlook is good; when it is part of a syndrome the prognosis is determined by the underlying disorder and its systemic complications.
pitfalls: Regarding it as invariably benign and failing to image the brain
Missing an underlying Joubert-related disorder with its renal and retinal risks
Overlooking ataxia-telangiectasia, with its important surveillance implications
Mistaking the compensatory head thrusts for a primary movement disorder
references: OMIM: Congenital Ocular Motor Apraxia, Cogan Type
management: No specific pharmacological therapy; isolated cases need reassurance, as the compensatory head thrusts tend to lessen with maturation
Early developmental intervention with physiotherapy and occupational therapy for associated gross motor delay
Investigate for an underlying cause with brain MRI, seeking the molar tooth sign of Joubert-related disorders, and targeted testing for ataxia-telangiectasia or the oculomotor-apraxia ataxias
Direct management according to any identified underlying syndrome and its systemic complications
Orthoptic and ophthalmological review to characterise the saccadic dysfunction and support visual function
Genetic counselling and ciliopathy-panel testing when a Joubert-related or other inherited disorder is confirmed
Longitudinal developmental and neurological monitoring to detect an evolving syndromic picture
